objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
question: Ibrahim, an office administrator at a law firm, has Claude review three competing copier service contracts so the partners can choose one at Friday's meeting. Which output format should he request?
options: A flowing narrative that discusses each contract in turn with full paragraphs of analysis
Three separate summaries produced in three separate conversations, one per contract
A single-paragraph verdict recommending one contract so the partners get a fast answer
A comparison table with the contracts as columns and consistent criteria — cost, response time, exit terms — as rows, since a side-by-side structure matches how the choice will be made
optionExplanations: Narrative buries the comparison: to weigh exit terms, the partners must hunt through three separate paragraphs and hold the figures in memory. Prose is the right format for argument and nuance, not for lining up three options against the same criteria.

Splitting the work across conversations guarantees inconsistency — each summary emphasizes different aspects, so the three outputs cannot be laid side by side. The comparison the partners need is exactly what three disconnected summaries fail to produce.

A verdict without visible trade-offs asks the partners to ratify a conclusion they cannot inspect, on a contract decision they own. The meeting needs the comparison itself; a recommendation can accompany it, but cannot replace it.

Correct. Format should mirror the decision structure: choosing among options against shared criteria is inherently tabular, and a table with consistent rows makes gaps, outliers, and trade-offs visible at a glance. Selecting structured output when the task is comparison is the core format-selection judgment.
principle: comparisons across options belong in a table
relatedConcept: Choose the output format that mirrors the task's structure — evaluating options against shared criteria calls for consistent side-by-side structure, not prose.
overallExplanation: Comparisons across options belong in a table: choose the output format that mirrors the task's structure, and evaluating options against shared criteria is inherently side-by-side.

objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
question: Lucia, a product-marketing associate at a pet-food brand, ran Claude's research mode on the raw-food segment and received a long, heavily sourced report. Leadership asked one question: should the brand enter this segment? What should Lucia do with the research output?
options: Curate before sharing: distill the findings that bear on the entry decision, keep the source links attached to the claims that survive, and cut the rest
Forward the complete report to leadership so that no potentially relevant finding is lost
Send leadership only the single-sentence bottom line so their time is fully respected
Convert the entire report, section by section, into a slide deck for the leadership meeting
optionExplanations: Correct. Curation is the step between research output and audience: selecting what bears on the actual decision, preserving the source links so surviving claims stay verifiable, and discarding the rest. The value Lucia adds is judgment about relevance — the raw report is input to her work, not the deliverable.

Forwarding everything transfers the curation work to the people with the least time to do it, and most of the report does not touch the entry decision. Completeness of the handoff is not a virtue when the question was specific; it is the absence of the analyst's job.

A bare yes-or-no strips out the reasoning and evidence leadership needs to weigh the call and probe its assumptions. Respecting their time means giving a decision-shaped brief with support, not withholding everything except the conclusion.

Reformatting is not curating: a slide per section faithfully reproduces the report's bulk in a different container, and the deck inherits every irrelevant passage as a slide. The problem to solve is selection, and changing the medium does not perform it.
principle: curate research to the decision, keep the sources
relatedConcept: Research output is raw material — the human's job is selecting what bears on the decision and preserving verifiability, not forwarding or reformatting the whole dump.
overallExplanation: Curate research to the decision, keep the sources: research output is raw material, and the human's job is selecting what bears on the decision while preserving verifiability.

objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
question: Ansel, a volunteer coordinator at a food bank, has finished developing a shift-onboarding checklist with Claude. The shift leads who will use it every weekend were not part of the conversation and need their own clean copy. What is the best way to deliver it?
options: Send the shift leads screenshots of the chat messages in which the checklist was worked out
Have Claude produce the checklist as an artifact — a standalone document he can copy, export, and share as a clean final version, separate from the conversation that produced it
Tell each shift lead to ask Claude to regenerate the checklist themselves whenever they need it
Paste the full conversation transcript into an email so the leads also see the reasoning behind each item
optionExplanations: Screenshots freeze the drafting process, not the deliverable: revisions scattered across messages mean the leads must reconstruct which version is final, and images of chat cannot be searched, printed cleanly, or updated. The working session is not the document.

Correct. The checklist's users live outside the conversation, so the content needs a container that travels: an artifact separates the finished deliverable from the chat that produced it, giving Ansel one authoritative version to copy, export, print, and distribute to the shift leads.

Each regeneration produces a fresh variant, so every shift lead would work from a slightly different checklist — and none from the version Ansel refined and approved. A vetted operational document must be distributed, not re-created on demand.

The transcript buries the checklist inside corrections, dead ends, and superseded drafts, leaving each reader to excavate the final version themselves. The leads need the outcome of the reasoning; shipping the whole process instead of the product serves no one.
principle: deliverables for people outside the chat need their own container
relatedConcept: When an output's users are not in the conversation, it belongs in an artifact — one authoritative, exportable version separated from the drafting process.
overallExplanation: Deliverables for people outside the chat need their own container: an artifact provides one authoritative, exportable version separated from the drafting process.

objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
question: Dario, a knowledge coordinator at an elevator-maintenance company, is consolidating findings from many Claude research sessions into a single reference page his field teams will consult. Which two practices will make the consolidated page most useful? (Choose two.)
options: Group the material by topic and by relevance to the teams' recurring tasks, rather than by the order in which the research happened
Include every finding gathered across all the sessions, so that no detail is ever lost
Keep source attributions attached to the claims so teammates can re-verify any item later
Merge everything into one continuous narrative so the page reads smoothly from start to finish
optionExplanations: Correct. Organization should serve the reader's retrieval pattern, not the researcher's history: field teams arrive with a task and need the relevant findings grouped where they will look. Chronological order preserves how the research unfolded, which is the one thing no user of the page cares about.

Including everything is hoarding, not curating — the marginal findings dilute the important ones, and a bloated page trains field teams to stop consulting it. Curation means the discipline of leaving things out; completeness of the archive belongs elsewhere.

Correct. A reference page outlives the sessions that fed it, and claims will eventually be questioned or need updating. Source attributions kept with each claim make every item independently re-verifiable later — traceability is what separates curated knowledge from unsourced folklore.

A continuous narrative optimizes for reading start-to-finish, which is exactly how a reference page is never used. Field teams scan and jump; headings, groups, and structure serve that access pattern, while smooth prose actively hides the item someone came to find.
principle: organize for retrieval, attribute for re-verification
relatedConcept: Curated reference material is grouped by how readers will look things up and keeps sources attached to claims — not everything, and not a narrative.
overallExplanation: Organize for retrieval, attribute for re-verification: curated reference material is grouped by how readers look things up, with sources kept attached to claims.
